title: Custom AI solutions: what should you walk away with?
description: Custom AI solutions: when to build or buy, what 9 AI models cost per typical job, and how to test any build.
verdict: Buy the AI model. Build only the part that holds your own data and workflow.[^4][^3]
Bought or partnered tools reached deployment about 67% of the time[^2], twice the internal-build rate, in one MIT study.[^1]
Custom usually means search over your own documents, not training a model. Search beats retraining for adding facts.[^5][^24]
Usage is cheap: $35 to $1,400 a month for 50,000 questions in our check. Upkeep is the hard part.[^17][^30]
Get it in writing: you own the prompts, test cases, search index, tuned models and code.[^13][^36]
summary: Custom AI solutions connect a bought model to your own data, rules and software, so AI drafts, finds and extracts from your documents.[^5][^6] Your staff check and decide.[^10] Testing on your own cases and planning upkeep make or break it.[^23][^30]
walkAway: You should leave with a build-or-buy call, a 3-year cost sheet, a test set from your files, an ownership contract and a named owner.[^3][^9]
A written build, buy or leave-it call for each use, with the off-the-shelf option tested first. Most AI uses at large firms are now bought, not built.[^3][^4]
A 3-year cost sheet: build, AI usage at dated list prices, upkeep and model changes. Gartner warns AI cost estimates can be off by 500% to 1,000%.[^9][^25]
A test set of 20 to 50 real cases from your files, with today's results and a pass mark agreed before any demo.[^23][^12]
A contract that says you own the prompts, test cases, search index, any tuned model and the code, and can take them with you.[^13][^36][^37]
A named owner who reruns the tests every month and whenever the vendor changes or retires a model.[^10][^12]
humanRole: Your people make the go or no-go call, set the right answers, settle ownership and approve customer-facing answers.[^10][^14]
The COO or process owner owns the result and makes the go or no-go call. NIST asks for checks by people who did not build the system.[^10]
A domain reviewer, such as the controller or an ops lead, sets the right answers and spot-checks output. Model makers say human judgment should calibrate any automated scoring.[^12][^23]

Your legal or contracts lead settles who owns data, outputs and any model tuned on your data before signing.[^13][^37] If the use is high-risk under EU rules, like hiring or credit, heavy changes can make your firm the legal provider.[^11]
Your firm stays liable for what its AI tells customers, so a named person approves customer-facing answers at launch.[^14]

recipes.name: 1. Answers from your own documents (the most common first build)
recipes.when: Pick this when staff hunt through manuals, contracts or specs for answers. Cloud providers advise starting with retrieval, which cites its sources and updates in minutes.[^5][^6]
flow: Ops lead: pick one document set and 20 to 50 real questions with known answers
Developer: build retrieval (search that hands the AI the right passages) on a bought model
IT lead: limit each person to the documents they can already open
Domain reviewer: grade answers against the test set and sign off
Ops lead: go live in one team first, then rerun the test set monthly
recipes.cost: Our check: $35 to $1,400 a month in AI usage for 50,000 questions.[^15][^17] A search index on Pinecone, a hosted search service, has a $50 monthly minimum on its Standard plan.[^21][^22]

recipes.name: 2. Pulling fields from documents into your system (batch work)
recipes.when: Pick this for forms, orders or statements that arrive in volume and can wait a day. All four providers we checked halve the price for batch work, with results within a day.[^15][^16]
flow: AP (accounts payable) lead or clerk: label 100 sample documents with the right fields
Developer: run batch extraction and score it against the labels
Reviewer: check low-confidence fields before anything posts
Controller: approve go-live once accuracy meets the agreed mark
recipes.cost: Our check: $3 (batch) to $240 a month in AI usage for 10,000 documents.[^15][^17] Labelling, review time and the link into your system cost more than the tokens.[^30]

recipes.name: 3. Tuning a model for format or sorting (only with many labelled examples)
recipes.when: Pick this for a stable task, like sorting tickets or a fixed output format, with many labelled past examples. Do not tune it to learn facts; retrieval does that better.[^6][^24]
flow: Ops lead: collect labelled past examples and hold some back for testing
Developer: tune a small model and compare it with the untuned one
Reviewer: check results on the held-back cases
Ops lead: plan a re-tune for when the base model retires
recipes.cost: OpenAI lists $5 to $25 per million training tokens, but it has closed fine-tuning to new customers.[^16] The bigger costs are labelling data and re-tuning after model retirements.[^26][^25]

ownData.title: What does a custom AI workload cost to run each month?
ownData.intro: About $35 to $1,400 a month for 50,000 questions by our math, depending on the model, at list prices read 26 Nov 2026.[^15][^16][^17] We priced two typical workloads on 9 models from 4 providers; a token, the unit AI is billed in, is about three-quarters of a word.[^18][^20] Worked example: 50,000 questions make 250 million tokens in, $500 at $2 per million, plus 20 million out, $200 at $10: $700 a month.
headers: Model (list price per million tokens, in / out)
10,000 documents a month (3,500 tokens in, 500 out each)
50,000 questions a month (5,000 tokens in, 400 out each)
50,000 questions over 3 years, at a flat price
rows: Google Gemini 4 Argon ($2 / $10 to 30 Nov 2026; $4 / $20 from 1 Dec 2026)[^17]
Mistral Large 4 ($0.70 / $2.10[^18], the higher of two official prices[^19])
ownData.note: Standard US list prices before tax, discounts and caching; token counts are our estimates, and the 3-year column assumes flat prices, which Google already breaks.[^20][^17] Excludes reasoning tokens, hosting, the search index, engineering and review time, and tests no quality: a cheap model may fail your test. Mistral's two official pages disagree on Large 4, so we used the higher; Google rows are the Gemini Developer API (application programming interface) paid tier.[^18][^19]

watchOuts: Most stall from building what could be bought, messy documents, model changes, unnoticed quality slips, weak contracts and cost surprises at volume.[^1][^8] Each fix is below.
Building what you could buy. Internal builds reached daily use about half as often as partnered ones, so test the off-the-shelf option on the same cases first.[^1][^4]
Messy or scattered documents. Most firms (63%) lack or are unsure of AI-ready data practices, so test on 50 real records before you build.[^8][^6]
Model retirements and price changes break the build. Two Google prices we checked double, on 1 Dec 2026 and 1 Jan 2027; vendors retire models on 2 to 6 months' notice.[^17][^25][^26][^27]
Quality slips without anyone noticing. Quality decayed over time in 91% of 128 model and dataset pairs in one study[^28], so rerun your test set monthly.[^29]
A contract that leaves the build with the vendor. Government buying guides say settle ownership, data rights and exit terms before signing.[^13][^36]
Cost surprises at full volume. Gartner warns cost estimates can be off by 500% to 1,000%, so price the pilot at real volume, not demo volume.[^9]
howToTest: Judge them by a test on your own cases: a pass mark set before the demo, run against an off-the-shelf tool and today's process.[^12][^23]
Write the pass mark before any demo, such as the share of fields that must be right, and require every answer to cite its source.[^38][^12]
Pull 20 to 50 real cases from your files, messy ones included, and keep them from the vendor until test day.[^23][^12]
Have two staff mark the right answers on their own, and drop cases they disagree on.[^23]
Run the custom build, an off-the-shelf tool and today's process on the same cases.[^10][^7]
Run each case more than once, since AI answers vary from run to run.[^23]
Ask the vendor in writing how they tested any accuracy claim, and on what data. The FTC has acted against AI accuracy claims made without solid evidence.[^39][^40]
Measure cost per case at your real volume, not just accuracy.[^9]
Price the lift in dollars: minutes saved x cases a month x loaded cost per minute (pay plus benefits). Subtract AI usage and upkeep.
Rerun the same set every month after go-live and whenever the model changes.[^12][^10]

faq.q: How much does custom AI development cost?
faq.a: AI projects reviewed on Clutch typically cost $10,000 to $49,999, and average about $120,600 over 10 months.[^41] Gartner puts an enterprise custom app at $750,000 to $1 million upfront; model usage ran just $35 to $1,400 a month in our check.[^42][^15][^17] Building, data preparation, testing and upkeep are the big costs, so ask for each priced separately.[^30][^9]

faq.q: Can I create my own custom AI?
faq.a: Yes, usually by connecting a bought model to your own documents, not by training one from scratch.[^5][^6] Google's engineers advise launching without machine learning until you have the data.[^7]

faq.q: Should we fine-tune on our documents or use RAG?
faq.a: Use RAG (retrieval-augmented generation: search that hands the AI the right passages). It beat fine-tuning (further training the model on your examples) for adding facts in a Microsoft study.[^24][^5] RAG also cites its sources; tune only for format or sorting.[^5][^6]

faq.q: Does the AI vendor train on our data, and who owns the output?
faq.a: No, not on paid business plans: Anthropic and OpenAI don't train on your content, and their terms say you own the outputs.[^31][^32][^33] Google's paid Gemini tier isn't used for training, but its free tier may be, so keep confidential files off it.[^35][^34]

faq.q: Should we build, buy or assemble AI solutions for our business?
faq.a: Buy the model, and build only the layer that holds your data and workflow.[^4][^1] In one investor's survey of US enterprise decision-makers, 76% of AI use cases were bought rather than built in 2025, up from 53%.[^3]

pickElse: When the job follows clear rules: use a rule or a no-code tool such as Zapier or Power Automate. Google says a simple rule often gets you about half the way.[^7]
Staff need drafting, summaries and search across email and files: buy seats of ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude for Work, Microsoft 365 Copilot or Gemini for Workspace.[^3][^1]
Your ERP (finance system) or CRM (customer database) already has AI built in: try it before building.[^4] Our AI integration guide shows what each system connects to.

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (Jul 2025)
sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Fortune, MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing (18 Aug 2025)
sources.what: Fortune's write-up of MIT NANDA's The GenAI Divide report. Headline: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing; about 5% of AI pilot programs achieve rapid revenue acceleration, while the vast majority stall with little to no measurable P&L impact. Purchasing AI tools from specialized vendors and building partnerships succeed about 67% of the time. Its comparison for internal builds misstates the report, where internal builds reach deployment about a third of the time: cite this write-up for the 67% and its headline figures only; MIT's report carries the internal-build rate and the "twice" comparison. Read 28 Nov 2026.

offer.heading: Not sure whether to build or buy?
offer.body: Buy the model and build only the part that holds your own data and workflow; if a product already does the job, buy it outright. In a free 30-minute call on your first workflow, you leave knowing whether to build, buy or leave it, and what it costs to run.

reviews.notes: Wanted a first workflow, a before-and-after measure and who does what. Roles are named in every recipe step; the test-set bullet now includes today's results, so there is a baseline to beat. Missing: a sourced time to build; the research found none neutral, so none is given.

Stalled on tokens, batch, fine-tuning and Pinecone. Token is now defined in the own-data intro, batch as results within a day, fine-tuning in the FAQ, Pinecone as a hosted search service. Moved the token counts per document and question into the table headers so the note stays short on a phone.

Asked whether one team can pilot first. The document-answers recipe now goes live in one team before rollout. Would like a figure for reviewer hours a week; nothing sourced exists, so the dollar formula in the test steps asks them to count it.

As the COO hiring the build: the 3-year column now says it assumes a flat price, and the Google rows show both prices and dates. Wanted the contract items concrete; walk-away and bottom line both list what to own. No neutral build-cost range exists, so the FAQ says so and asks for each part priced separately.

Steve's worries: data, security, skills, return, consultant fees. Data has its own watch-out; security is the vendor-training FAQ and the IT access step; return is the dollar formula. Cut 'thin layer' and 'document index' from the bottom line as jargon. No Zavient fee shown, since prices are not set; offer says no sales pitch.

answers.walk-away: Walk away with a build-or-buy call per use, a 3-year cost sheet, a test set of real cases, a contract saying you own the work, and a named owner.[^3][^9][^23][^13][^10]
answers.human-role: The COO or process owner makes the go or no-go call, a domain reviewer spot-checks output, and a named person approves customer-facing answers.[^10][^12][^14]
answers.recipes: Custom AI work takes three common shapes: answers from your own documents, pulling fields from documents into your system, or tuning a model for format or sorting.[^5][^15][^6]
answers.what-goes-wrong: Pilots stall when firms build what they could buy, start with messy documents, or stop testing as models change and quality slips.[^1][^8][^25][^28]
answers.benchmark: Judge an advisor by whether they set a pass mark before any demo, test on 20 to 50 of your own cases, and compare against off-the-shelf tools.[^38][^23][^10]
answers.something-else: Don't hire help when a rule or no-code tool does the job, bought seats cover drafting and search, or your ERP or CRM already has AI built in.[^7][^3][^4]
